Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SNMP sweep from external source using default community strings (FSB Center 16 recon) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco Smart Install exploitation (CVE-2018-0171) — inbound TCP/4786 from untrusted source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Network device configuration exfiltration via SNMP config-copy / TFTP-FTP egress (Static Tundra) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Cisco Smart Install exploitation (CVE-2018-0171) — inbound TCP/4786 from untrusted source AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound TCP port 4786 (Cisco Smart Install / SMI) traffic reaching network infrastructure from external or untrusted source IPs, the entry vector FSB Center 16 (Static Tundra) uses to trigger config extraction and RCE on unpatched Cisco IOS/IOS-XE devices per the FBI advisory referenced in this article. Article-specific because it targets the exact CVE (CVE-2018-0171) and Smart Install protocol the FSB actors abuse, not generic scanning. Rationale: Uses CVE-2018-0171 and its fixed protocol port (Cisco Smart Install / TCP 4786) named in the FBI advisory the article cites; SMI has no legitimate internet-facing use, so external inbound 4786 is high-fidelity. Defender KQL left empty because the targets are Cisco routers/switches, not Defender-managed endpoints. Corroborated via FBI IC3 PSA and Cisco Talos Static Tundra reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2025/russian-government-cyber-actors-targeting-networking-devices-critical-infrastructure • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2018-0171 • https://research.splunk.com/stories/cisco_smart_install_remote_code_execution_cve-2018-0171/
ATT&CKT1190 T1602.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing 4786 from an internal scanning subnet
  • Cisco DNA Center / Prime Infrastructure legitimately using Smart Install from a management station
  • External security-research internet scanners (Shodan/Censys) hitting a perimeter device
  • Penetration-test engagement using smi_check / SIET tooling
  • Misconfigured management traffic traversing an untrusted transit link
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<add authorized scanner IPs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted and identify the DestinationIP device model and IOS version; check if Smart Install is enabled (`show vstack config`) and whether the device is unpatched for CVE-2018-0171. 2) Contain: block TCP/4786 at the perimeter, disable Smart Install (`no vstack`) on the device, and rotate device credentials/SNMP strings. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'SNMP config exfiltration' and 'SNMP scanning' from the same SourceIP; review the device running-config for unauthorized ACL/local-account/TFTP changes and evidence of SYNful Knock implants.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 4786
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Targets=make_set(DestinationIP, 50) by SourceIP, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by Attempts desc

Network device configuration exfiltration via SNMP config-copy / TFTP-FTP egress (Static Tundra) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts network devices copying their running-config off-box to an external host over TFTP/FTP, or Cisco syslog referencing the attacker config filenames config.bkp/output.txt — the SNMP config-copy MIB exfiltration technique FSB Center 16 uses to collect device configurations en masse. Article-specific: mirrors the advisory's 'copy its configuration to a file and transfer it to an attacker-controlled VPS or compromised FTP server' behaviour. Rationale: Combines the advisory's exact exfil filenames (config.bkp / output.txt) and the SNMP config-copy-to-TFTP/FTP behaviour from CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB; a router/switch pushing running-config to a public IP over TFTP(69)/FTP(21) is rare and high-signal. Sigma omitted because the highest-fidelity form (Cisco syslog string match + external-egress correlation) is not a clean single-event standard logsource. Corroborated via MITRE T1602.002 and Cisco Talos Static Tundra reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1602/002/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://industrialcyber.co/threats-attacks/russian-fsb-center-16-exploits-decade-old-cisco-flaw-in-cyber-espionage-campaign-to-target-critical-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1602.002 T1602.001 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled network backup jobs (SolarWinds NCM, RANCID, Oxidized) legitimately copying configs — but normally to an INTERNAL server
  • Admin manually running `copy running-config tftp:` to an authorized internal TFTP host
  • Firmware/IOS image staging over TFTP during a maintenance window
  • A misconfigured backup target pointing at a cloud/public IP
  • IPAM or monitoring tooling pulling configs via SNMP for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("<approved-tftp-server-ip>", "oxidized", "rancid", "solarwinds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source device and destination IP; confirm the destination is external and NOT an approved config-backup server, and check whether the copy used config.bkp/output.txt naming. 2) Contain: null-route/block the external destination, revoke SNMP write access and rotate all SNMP community strings, and isolate the device for forensic capture of running vs startup config. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC 'Cisco Smart Install exploitation' and 'SNMP scanning' from the same actor infrastructure; enumerate every device whose config left the org in the same window and check for unauthorized accounts/ACL/GRE-tunnel changes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("config.bkp", "output.txt")
    or (SyslogMessage has "running-config" and SyslogMessage has_any ("tftp", "ftp") and SyslogMessage has_any ("copy", "ccCopy"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SNMP sweep from external source using default community strings (FSB Center 16 recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single external source IP issuing SNMP (UDP/161) requests against many internal network devices — the proxy-fronted SNMP scanning FSB Center 16 uses to find poorly configured devices that accept common/default community strings before pulling their configs. Article-specific: models the advisory's 'scan for Internet IP ranges with active SNMP agents that accept common or default community strings' step. Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's SNMP v1/v2 default-community-string scanning: one external source touching >=25 distinct internal SNMP agents (UDP/161) is a scan, not management. Threshold-based aggregation so Sigma is intentionally skipped. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because SNMP scanning of network gear surfaces on firewall/flow telemetry, not endpoint EDR or AWS logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1602/001/ • https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jul/09/2003959498/-1/-1/0/CSA_IMPROVE_ROUTER_HYGIENE.PDF
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1602.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized NMS/monitoring platform (SolarWinds, PRTG, LibreNMS, Zabbix) polling many devices over SNMP — normally from an internal poller, not external
  • Approved external managed-service provider (MSP) monitoring the estate over SNMP
  • Vulnerability scanner performing SNMP enumeration during a sanctioned assessment
  • Internet-wide research scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching perimeter interfaces
  • IPAM/asset-discovery tool running a scheduled SNMP inventory sweep
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<approved-external-MSP-poller-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate/enrich SourceIP (ASN, threat-intel, proxy/VPN reputation) and confirm it is not an approved internal or MSP poller; note how many and which device types were swept. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, migrate devices to SNMPv3 with authPriv, and remove default/common community strings (public/private). 3) Hunt: check whether any swept device subsequently exported its config (UC 'config exfiltration') or received inbound TCP/4786 (UC 'Smart Install'); treat any device that responded to a default community string as potentially enumerated and audit its running-config.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0171", "CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0171", "CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser/Node contact with Lucide student-proxy DDoS campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the Lucide (lucideproxy) campaign's clustered infrastructure — the Wisp flood endpoint lunaron[.]top, the still-live monetization/script hosts, and the G-Core Labs IP that fronted 90 of 93 deployment hostnames. Article-specific because these exact domains/IP are JFrog+SafeDep-confirmed campaign IOCs with no legitimate business use. Rationale: Pivots on the exact JFrog/SafeDep-confirmed campaign endpoints — Wisp flood host lunaron[.]top, monetization hosts woofbeginner[.]com and c.vipersfutbol[.]com the current build still reaches, commit-email domain geeked[.]wtf, and the G-Core IP 92.38.177[.]17 that resolved 90 of 93 deployment hostnames. None have legitimate enterprise use, so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://safedep.io/malicious-npm-terminal3airport-proxy-adware-spam/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-148-malicious-npm-packages-masquerading-as-student-proxies-turn-browsers-into-ddos-botnet
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or SOC analyst deliberately detonating the proxy in a sandbox that ships telemetry to the same tenant
  • Threat-intel or URL-scanning tooling (urlscan.io agent, VirusTotal retro-hunt box) resolving the domains for enrichment
  • A student personal device on guest WiFi loading the proxy site (expected true positive, but low security impact vs corporate asset)
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup as an outbound event
  • Passive-DNS or newly-registered-domain feed pre-fetching the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan.exe", "vt-cli.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs node vs script engine) and confirm the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP matches a campaign IOC, not a lookalike; check whether the connection succeeded or was blocked at proxy/firewall. 2) Contain: block all five IOCs (lunaron.top, woofbeginner.com, c.vipersfutbol.com, geeked.wtf, 92.38.177.17) at DNS/egress, and on the affected browser clear cache + local storage and unregister any service worker registered by a tutoring/proxy domain. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host for npm installs of the named packages (UC2) and for sustained connection floods to lunaron.top or cdn.caan.edu (UC3/UC4); check whether any build agent pulled the packages into a lockfile.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("lunaron.top", "woofbeginner.com", "c.vipersfutbol.com", "geeked.wtf")
    or RemoteIP == "92.38.177.17"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any ("lunaron.top", "woofbeginner.com", "c.vipersfutbol.com", "geeked.wtf")
 | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Indicator = Name, Src = "DNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any ("lunaron.top", "woofbeginner.com", "c.vipersfutbol.com", "geeked.wtf")
     or DestinationIP == "92.38.177.17"
     or RequestURL has_any ("lunaron.top", "woofbeginner.com", "c.vipersfutbol.com")
 | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Indicator = DestinationHostName, Src = "Proxy/FW")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of named Lucide malicious student-proxy npm packages AIDelivery High
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm installs or node_modules writes of the specific packages JFrog flagged as still-malicious in the campaign — charlie-kirk, ilovefemboys, miguelphonk. Article-specific because these package names are named IOCs; charlie-kirk was still serving malicious versions 2.0.0 and 3.0.1 as of 2026-07-14. Rationale: Uses the three package names the article explicitly cites (charlie-kirk, ilovefemboys, miguelphonk), gated on package-manager execution context so it fires on the actual dependency pull, not incidental text. High fidelity because these are confirmed IOCs and charlie-kirk was verified still-malicious on 2026-07-14. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://safedep.io/malicious-npm-terminal3airport-proxy-adware-spam/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally cloning the malicious package for reverse-engineering / IOC extraction
  • A security scanner (Snyk, npm audit, SafeDep pmg) enumerating the package name in its own log line
  • An internal wiki/ticket automation that echoes the package name into a build script comment
  • A legitimately-named unrelated future package reusing 'charlie-kirk' after the malicious ones are purged (verify version 2.0.0/3.0.1)
  • Grep/security-tooling output that references the string in a scan result rather than an install

| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("snyk", "npm audit", "pmg", "safedep") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("snyk.exe", "trivy.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command was an actual install (npm install / add) and capture the resolved version — versions 2.0.0 and 3.0.1 of charlie-kirk are the confirmed-malicious ones; check the host's package-lock.json/pnpm-lock.yaml for the entry. 2) Contain: remove the package from manifests and lockfiles, delete the node_modules copy, and rebuild clean; if the artifact was served anywhere, block the campaign domains at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether any browser/CI process on the host later contacted lunaron.top or cdn.caan.edu (UC1/UC3/UC4), and sweep the org's lockfiles for all 148 package names from JFrog's list.

Browser HTTP flood against nursing-school domain cdn.caan.edu AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a compromised browser tab acting as a Lucide DDoS bot: the G2 loader's archived payload fired a fresh one-million-character no-cors POST at cdn.caan.edu every 500ms. Detects sustained high-count outbound connections to caan.edu from a browser process — a rate no human browsing produces. Rationale: Grounded in the archived May-30 G2 payload JFrog recovered: a no-cors POST of a one-million-character string to cdn.caan.edu every 500ms (~2 MB/s per tab). The count threshold captures the automated flood cadence while the browser-process gate excludes server-side traffic — a shape no legitimate user generates against a single nursing-school CDN. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-148-malicious-npm-packages-masquerading-as-student-proxies-turn-browsers-into-ddos-botnet
ATT&CKT1498.001 T1583.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate student/staff member of Chamberlain/CAAN nursing programs heavily using cdn.caan.edu courseware (verify request cadence and payload size)
  • A synthetic-monitoring or uptime probe pointed at caan.edu from a corporate browser-automation host
  • A load/performance test a partner org runs against caan.edu with authorization
  • Browser prefetch/prerender inflating connection counts on a single legitimate page visit
  • A shared NAT/proxy egress IP aggregating many users' normal traffic to caan.edu above the threshold (pivot on SourceHostName not SourceIP)
Suppression filter
| where SourceHostName !has "synthetic" and SourceHostName !has "loadtest"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser is the initiator and the connection rate/payload matches a flood (hundreds of POSTs, ~2 MB/s upload) rather than normal courseware use; identify what page/tab the user had open. 2) Contain: block cdn.caan.edu and the campaign domains at egress, kill the offending browser tab/process, and clear the browser's cache, local storage and any tutoring/proxy service worker. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the Wisp flood to lunaron.top (UC4) and for the npm package install (UC2); notify caan.edu's abuse contact if your egress contributed to their flood.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "caan.edu"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
| summarize connCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 5)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| where connCount > 100    // script POSTs every 500ms -> >100 conns within minutes; humans never sustain this to one edu host
| order by connCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "caan.edu" or RequestURL has "caan.edu"
| summarize reqCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Methods = make_set(RequestMethod, 5)
    by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName
| where reqCount > 100    // sustained flood; 500ms POST cadence far exceeds any human page load
| order by reqCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(cdn.caan.edu OR *.caan.edu) @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/caan\.edu$/i ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=connCount)) | connCount > 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count as connCount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="*caan.edu" AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where connCount > 100 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - connCount
| tstats summariesonly=false count as connCount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="*caan.edu" AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where connCount > 100 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - connCount
Browser Wisp/WebSocket control-plane flood to Lucide endpoint lunaron.top AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the I2 module's control-plane attack: each infected browser opened up to 1,024 (config: 30) staggered WebSocket connections to a Wisp endpoint on lunaron.top and hammered it with CONNECT/CLOSE frames every 100ms. Detects an abnormal burst of concurrent connections from one browser to lunaron.top / the campaign IP — the socket-exhaustion signature. Rationale: Uses the JFrog-reconstructed I2 config values verbatim — a Wisp WebSocket target on lunaron[.]top with a per-browser socket count of 30 (cap 1,024) — and the G-Core IP 92.38.177[.]17. A browser opening 30+ concurrent sockets to one host and holding them is the socket-exhaustion control-plane signature, not human browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/150-npm-packages-promises-wi-fi-bypass-students/
ATT&CKT1498.001 T1499.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A browser with many tabs to a single legitimate high-concurrency web app (SPA with websockets, video conferencing) crossing 30 concurrent sockets — but not to lunaron.top
  • A shared NAT egress IP aggregating multiple browsers' connections (pivot on SourceHostName/DeviceName, not SourceIP)
  • A researcher detonating the proxy in a monitored VM
  • Connection-pooling proxies that multiplex and inflate observed connection counts to the campaign IP
  • The campaign IP later reassigned by G-Core to a benign tenant (re-validate the IP is still campaign-attributed before alerting)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-analysis"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 30+ concurrent connections originate from one browser process to lunaron.top / 92.38.177.17 and are sustained (Wisp CONNECT/CLOSE every 100ms), not a one-off burst; identify the open tab. 2) Contain: block lunaron.top and 92.38.177.17 at egress, terminate the browser process/tab, and clear the browser cache, local storage and any tutoring/proxy service worker. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the parallel cdn.caan.edu HTTP flood (UC3), the initial npm package install (UC2), and sweep egress for other hosts hitting the campaign IP; report the abusive Wisp traffic if lunaron.top is a third-party victim.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "lunaron.top" or RemoteIP == "92.38.177.17"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
| summarize connCount = count(), DistinctPorts = dcount(LocalPort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| where connCount > 30    // archived Wisp config aimed each browser at 30 sockets (cap 1024)
| order by connCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "lunaron.top" or DestinationIP == "92.38.177.17"
| summarize connCount = count(), DistinctSrcPorts = dcount(SourcePort), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName
| where connCount > 30    // Wisp config: 30 concurrent sockets per browser
| order by connCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:(lunaron.top OR *.lunaron.top) OR @DestinationIp:92.38.177.17) @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="92.38.177.17" ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=connCount)) | connCount > 30
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count as connCount dc(All_Traffic.src_port) as srcPorts min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="lunaron.top" OR All_Traffic.dest="92.38.177.17") AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where connCount > 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - connCount
| tstats summariesonly=false count as connCount dc(All_Traffic.src_port) as srcPorts min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="lunaron.top" OR All_Traffic.dest="92.38.177.17") AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where connCount > 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - connCount
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",

                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

status: experimental

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated Salesforce Aura/GraphQL guest scraping past 2,000-record limit · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export · [LLM] Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) · [LLM] Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts OAuth consent grants inside Salesforce to a connected app branded as 'Data Loader' but not the legitimate Salesforce client, the payoff of the ShinyHunters/UNC6040 vishing calls. Surfaces the granting user, source IP and geo so an analyst can confirm the call/consent chain. Rationale: Keys on the article's explicit lure — a connected app 'dressed up as Salesforce's own Data Loader tool' — corroborated by GTIG/Mandiant which note the consented app's name/branding differs from the legit Data Loader. Consent event ties the malicious app to a specific user identity, IP and geo. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250912.pdf • https://appomni.com/blog/detecting-unc6040-vishing-in-salesforce-oauth-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1078.004 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately installing/authorizing the genuine Salesforce Data Loader connected app for data migration
  • Data migration or ETL project onboarding a Data Loader-style integration
  • Sandbox refresh where connected apps are re-consented
  • Third-party MSP performing an authorized bulk data load
  • Renamed internal integration that happens to contain 'Data Loader' in its label
Suppression filter
| where not (ConsentedApp has "Data Loader" and IsAdminOperation == true and CountryCode in ("US","GB"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the consenting user and confirm out-of-band whether they authorized a Data Loader app in the last 24h; check if the client_id matches Salesforce's official Data Loader vs an arbitrary/attacker app id and whether a vishing call preceded it. 2) Contain: in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, revoke the app's tokens and block the app; force re-auth / reset the user's session. 3) Hunt: review that app's ApiEvent/BulkApi activity for enumeration and secret-hunting SOQL, and check for other users who consented to the same app id.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent","Connected","OAuth","Authorize","Grant")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ConsentedApp = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ConnectedAppName), ObjectName)
| where ConsentedApp has "Data Loader"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ConsentedApp, ObjectId
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts high-volume SOQL/Bulk-API data pulls performed by trusted vendor connected apps named Drift, Gainsight or Klue — the integrations whose stolen OAuth/refresh tokens ShinyHunters (UNC6395/Storm-3138) turned against downstream Salesforce orgs. Flags export volume far above a normal integration sync. Rationale: Names the exact compromised vendor apps from the article (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue) and thresholds on export volume — the Drift token theth alone reportedly exposed 700+ orgs by querying/exporting Salesforce objects, so bulk row counts by these apps are high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1530 T1567
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled Gainsight/Drift sync ingesting large object volumes after a new deployment
  • Initial full-history backfill when a vendor integration is first connected
  • Analytics/BI vendor app running a large nightly report export
  • Data migration event temporarily spiking a vendor app's query volume
  • Sandbox seeding where a vendor app bulk-reads production data
Suppression filter
| where not (AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue") and SrcIps has_any ("<known-vendor-egress-range>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the connected app and compare the query volume and source IP/ASN to its 30-day baseline; confirm whether the vendor has disclosed a token-theft incident (Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue advisories). 2) Contain: revoke the app's OAuth/refresh tokens in Salesforce Connected Apps OAuth Usage and disable the integration user; rotate any credentials the exported objects could contain. 3) Hunt: pivot to the SOQL bodies for secret-hunting patterns (AWS/Snowflake), and check for query-job deletions the actor uses to cover tracks.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Bulk","Report","Export","Query")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend AppName = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ClientName))
| where AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue")
| extend Rows = toint(coalesce(Raw.RowsProcessed, Raw.NumberOfRecords, Raw.RowCount))
| summarize TotalRows = sum(Rows), Queries = count(), SrcIps = make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AppName, AccountDisplayName
| where TotalRows > 50000 or Queries > 500   // 50k rows / 500 calls = well above a normal chat/CI integration sync cadence
| order by TotalRows desc

Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SOQL/API queries whose body searches Salesforce records (support cases, notes) for embedded secrets — AWS access keys, Snowflake tokens, VPN and password strings — exactly the loot UNC6395 sifted for after stealing Drift tokens. Content match on the AKIA prefix and secret keywords. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit statement that operators ran SOQL to sift support cases for AWS keys, Snowflake tokens and passwords; the AWS 'AKIA' access-key prefix plus 'snowflakecomputing' are low-FP content anchors that ordinary CRM queries rarely contain. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running a legitimate secret-sprawl audit across Salesforce records
  • DLP or CASB vendor scanning case bodies for exposed credentials
  • Support agent legitimately searching a case containing the word 'password'
  • Integration that indexes case text for search and echoes keywords in query logs
  • Pentest/red-team engagement authorized to hunt for embedded secrets
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("dlp","casb","secaudit") or IsAdminOperation == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full SOQL body and the querying identity/app — confirm whether the actor is a vendor integration token (see Drift/Gainsight/Klue) or an interactive session, and whether results returned rows. 2) Contain: revoke the querying app/user tokens and immediately rotate any AWS keys, Snowflake tokens or VPN creds that were stored in the matched objects. 3) Hunt: enumerate all objects returned, check for downstream use of the harvested keys in AWS CloudTrail/Snowflake login history, and look for query-job deletion covering the activity.

Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts deletion/abort of Salesforce async query, Apex and Bulk-API job records — the track-covering step the Salesloft Drift operators used, deleting their query jobs to slow investigators. Keys on delete/abort actions targeting job objects rather than a bare column. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated anti-forensic behaviour ('deleting their query jobs to slow down anyone investigating'); scopes to async/bulk job object types so it fires on evidence removal, not routine record deletes. Fixes prior schema error by matching on ActionType values instead of a non-existent 'Delete' column. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion
ATT&CKT1070 T1070.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin housekeeping that clears completed/failed async Apex jobs
  • Bulk-API integration aborting a stuck or duplicate job
  • Scheduled cleanup script pruning old BackgroundOperation records
  • DevOps pipeline aborting bulk loads during a failed deployment
  • Salesforce support aborting a runaway job during a case
Suppression filter
| where not (IsAdminOperation == true and AccountDisplayName has_any ("integration","svc","automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who deleted/aborted the job and whether the same identity ran large SOQL/Bulk exports just before the deletion (correlate on user/app + preceding 1h). 2) Contain: preserve remaining Real-Time Event Monitoring logs, revoke the identity's tokens, and enable log export/retention to prevent further tampering. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the deleted jobs' query scope from surviving ApiEvent/BulkApi telemetry and check for secret-hunting SOQL and vendor-token abuse by the same actor.

Unauthenticated Salesforce Aura/GraphQL guest scraping past 2,000-record limit AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated guest-user hits to the Salesforce Experience Cloud Aura endpoint (/s/sfsites/aura) using cursor-based GraphQL pagination and modified AuraInspector tooling to pull records beyond the 2,000-row cap. Best expressed on WAF/proxy web logs fronting the Experience Cloud site. Rationale: Uses the concrete guest-access endpoint /s/sfsites/aura and the named AuraInspector tooling from the article and GTIG's AuraInspector write-up; cursor-paginated volume past the 2,000-record cap gives a clean threshold on scraping vs. normal public-site browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/auditing-salesforce-aura-data-exposure • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/salesforce-graphql-guest-user-exploit-key-actions-to-take • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/salesforce-graphql-exploit-explained/
ATT&CKT1213 T1530 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate security team running the original Mandiant AuraInspector to audit their own guest exposure
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring hitting the Experience Cloud site repeatedly
  • SEO crawler or archiver paginating public community content
  • Load test against the Experience Cloud site
  • Vendor security scan authorized against the public site
Suppression filter
| where not (UA has "AuraInspector" and SourceIP in ("<internal-security-scanner-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP/ASN is external and unauthenticated, and check whether the guest profile has 'API Enabled' plus over-broad object/field permissions on the queried objects. 2) Contain: remove 'API Enabled' from the guest user profile, tighten guest object/field-level security and sharing rules, and block the scraping IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: quantify which objects/records were exposed via the Aura/GraphQL responses, review other Experience Cloud sites in the org for the same misconfig, and search for the same UA/IP across tenants.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend Uri = tostring(coalesce(Raw.Uri, Raw.RequestUrl, Raw.Page))
| where Uri has "/s/sfsites/aura" or Uri has "aura?r="
| where AccountType has_any ("Guest","Anonymous","Unauthenticated") or UserAgent has "AuraInspector"
| summarize Requests = count(), Uris = dcount(Uri), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, UserAgent, CountryCode, ISP
| where Requests > 200   // cursor-paginated scraping (2000-row pages) far exceeds human browsing of a public site
| order by Requests desc

| where Requests > 200   // high-volume cursor pagination of the guest Aura endpoint
   or UA has "AuraInspector"
| order by Requests desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimai authenticated session activity with no preceding form-login POST (forged remember-me cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Kimai (Symfony) authenticated access to admin/API/user routes from a source IP that never submitted a POST to the login form in the lookback window. CVE-2026-52824 lets an attacker with the publicly-known default APP_SECRET forge the KIMAI_REMEMBER cookie and be silently auto-authenticated, so the account 'logs in' without any credential submission crossing the wire. Rationale: Uses Kimai's KIMAI_REMEMBER remember-me cookie name and Symfony's form-login POST as the two anchors from the article; the anti-join (authenticated route access from an IP that never POSTed to login) is the observable footprint of a forged remember-me cookie since Symfony auto-authenticates without a credential exchange. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and Symfony login docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'remember me' users whose original POST /login happened before the lookback window began
  • SSO / reverse-proxy that terminates auth upstream and forwards without a Kimai form POST
  • Corporate NAT egress where one IP both logs in and is reused by an automation account
  • Health-check / monitoring probes hitting /api with a stored service session
  • Load balancer or CDN rewriting the client source IP so the login POST and the app request appear on different IPs
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "kube-probe" and CIp !in (dynamic(["<corporate-egress-not-needed:leave-empty-or-populate-org-CIDRs-in-loginIPs-let>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CIp's full request timeline; confirm the first authenticated request truly has no prior POST to /login and inspect whether Cookie carried KIMAI_REMEMBER but never a fresh PHPSESSID handshake. Identify which Kimai account (CsUsername) the session maps to and whether it is super_admin. 2) Contain: rotate APP_SECRET immediately (invalidates all forged cookies/links), force-logout all sessions, and require password reset + enable 2FA on privileged accounts. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA hit login-link URLs (hash/expires/user params) or created users, changed rates, or exported timesheets; confirm the instance was on Kimai < 2.58.0 with the default secret.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let loginIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where CsMethod == "POST" and CsUriStem has "login"   // Kimai/Symfony form-login check route
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/admin/", "/api/", "/user")   // authenticated Kimai surfaces
| where ScStatus >= 200 and ScStatus < 400
| where CsUsername != "" or Cookie has "KIMAI_REMEMBER"    // session was authenticated
| where CIp !in (loginIPs)                                 // but no form login ever seen from this IP
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20) by CIp, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Kimai forged Symfony login-link request (user+expires+hash signed URL) to super_admin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound GET requests whose query string carries the Symfony passwordless login-link signature triad — user, expires and hash. With the default APP_SECRET (CVE-2026-52824) an unauthenticated attacker can mint valid login links for any account, so a burst of these signed URLs (especially targeting the id=1/super_admin identifier) from external IPs is a direct forgery indicator. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'LoginLink signatures' forgery vector and the Symfony-documented login-link parameter triad (user/expires/hash); matching all three tokens in the query string is a distinctive single-event signature that fires even without knowing Kimai's exact check-route path. Cross-checked Symfony login-link docs and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation legitimately uses Symfony/Kimai passwordless login links for real users
  • Password-reset or email-verification links that reuse a similar signed-URL shape
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP) fuzzing query parameters named user/expires/hash
  • Uptime monitors replaying a captured login-link URL
  • Other Symfony apps behind the same proxy emitting UriSigner-style links
Suppression filter
| where CsUriStem !has "password-reset" and UserAgent !has_any ("ZAP", "Burp", "Nuclei", "masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract TargetUser from CsUriQuery; determine whether the value corresponds to the id=1/super_admin username and whether the request returned 200/302 (link accepted). Check the source IP's geo/ASN and whether it is external. 2) Contain: if the login link was accepted, rotate APP_SECRET (invalidates every forged link), kill active sessions, reset the targeted account's password and enforce 2FA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same CIp/UA for subsequent authenticated admin/API activity and for KIMAI_REMEMBER-cookie sessions; verify the deployment ran the default APP_SECRET on Kimai < 2.58.0.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriQuery has "hash=" and CsUriQuery has "expires=" and CsUriQuery has "user="   // Symfony login-link signed URL triad
| extend TargetUser = extract(@"(?i)user=([^&]+)", 1, CsUriQuery)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, UserAgent, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, TargetUser, ScStatus, CsUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site
Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm dropping its self-replicating payload and CI persistence file onto developer machines during npm install. Fires on the confirmed malicious bundle.js SHA256 or the distinctive worm filenames written by node/npm. Rationale: Uses the second-source-confirmed Shai-Hulud bundle.js SHA256 (46faab8a...) and the campaign's distinctive filenames (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) named across Unit42/Wiz/Datadog write-ups of the article's flagship campaign; hash+filename anchors make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named a file bundle.js under a non-malicious .github/workflows path (rare — that dir holds YAML, not JS)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the payload re-triggering the file-write event from the quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel/IR team staging IOC files named setup_bun.js for tabletop or purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows Defender\", @"\Quarantine\") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName node.exe/npm) and the folder — a real hit is bundle.js/setup_bun.js executed during an npm/bun install in a repo working dir. Check the file SHA256 against 46faab8a... 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, revoke and rotate all npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) keys used from it; check GitHub for a newly-created public repo named 'Shai-Hulud' and any 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' pushed to your repos. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to webhook.site from the same host, enumerate every package version installed in the last 24h, and scope other developers who installed the same dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileSHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud npm Worm Payload and Workflow File Written
id: 6f2c1e94-8a13-4b77-9d2e-7c5a1f0b3d21
description: Detects the Shai-Hulud self-replicating npm worm dropping its payload (bundle.js) or CI persistence/2.0 payload files on disk
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/aikido-intel-detects-malware-vulnerabilities-first
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_hash:
    Hashes|contains: '46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09'
  selection_names:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\shai-hulud-workflow.yml'
      - '\setup_bun.js'
      - '\bun_environment.js'
  condition: selection_hash or selection_names
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\shai-hulud-workflow.yml OR *\setup_bun.js OR *\bun_environment.js OR *\Setup_Bun.js) OR @Hashes:*46FAAB8AB153FAE6E80E7CCA38EAB363075BB524EDD79E42269217A083628F09*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(shai-hulud-workflow\.yml|setup_bun\.js|bun_environment\.js)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js") OR Filesystem.file_hash="46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09" OR (Filesystem.file_name="bundle.js" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\workflows\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js") OR Filesystem.file_hash="46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09" OR (Filesystem.file_name="bundle.js" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\workflows\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's credential exfiltration stage where the postinstall payload beacons harvested npm/GitHub/cloud tokens to the hardcoded webhook.site drop (bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Pairs the webhook.site destination with a node/npm/bun/git initiating process to cut the FP from legit webhook testing. Rationale: Anchors on the second-source-confirmed hardcoded exfil host webhook.site (Shai-Hulud endpoint bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) but requires a node/npm/bun/git initiating process so it fires on postinstall exfil, not a developer manually testing a webhook in a browser. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using webhook.site to test an outbound webhook from a Node app during development
  • CI runner (node/git) hitting a webhook.site URL configured in a test suite or integration fixture
  • QA automation posting to webhook.site as a capture endpoint
  • Internal tooling that uses webhook.site free-tier bins for prototyping event delivery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","ci","exec") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-agent","ci-runner") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "jenkins")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RemoteUrl/DNS path — a real hit posts to a webhook.site UUID bin (campaign default bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) shortly after an npm/bun install; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for a package install and correlate with a bundle.js/setup_bun.js write in the last hour. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, immediately rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and AWS/GCP/Azure keys from that machine, and block webhook.site at egress. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit for a new public 'Shai-Hulud' repo or 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' commits under affected users, and scope every other host that installed the same package version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

        Image|endswith:

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
