File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-13 15 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified threat actor activity with overlapping tradecraft commonly associated with ShinyHunters, including voice phishing (vishing), supply-chain compromise, and misconfigured guest access targeting SaaS-based applications. The post Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs · [LLM] Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration · [LLM] Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Salesforce API/CRM query activity attributed to a Connected App originating from the specific source IPs Microsoft tied to ShinyHunters/UNC6395 abuse of trusted OAuth integrations (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue). Because the actors ride sanctioned OAuth tokens, IP is the highest-fidelity anchor available on this telemetry. Rationale: Anchors on the five Microsoft-published IOC IPs (article Table 2; 138.226.246.94 is explicitly the Klue integration performing CRM API queries) scoped to Salesforce API/Connected-App activity — a fixed IP set on SaaS API telemetry is an alerting-grade match with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
ATT&CKT1199 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate integration vendor (Klue/Gainsight) re-uses one of these IPs post-remediation for sanctioned traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally shares an IP block with a listed address
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs or a SOC replay hitting the Salesforce API from a sinkholed IP
  • Security researcher / IR team validating the IOC against the tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all CloudAppEvents for the matched IP, note the ConnectedAppId and AccountDisplayName acting on its behalf, and confirm whether the app is an approved Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue integration. 2) Contain: in Salesforce, revoke the Connected App's OAuth tokens and block the source IP at the org login-IP-range/Connected-App policy; rotate the integration's connection secret. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ReportExport/BulkApi call by that ConnectedAppId, pivot to other tenants/users the same app touched, and search for the remaining four IOC IPs and any credentials exposed in exported records.
let IocIps = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in (IocIps)
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), ConnectedApps=make_set(ConnectedAppId,10), Users=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Events desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let IocIps = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in (IocIps)
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), ConnectedApps=make_set(ConnectedAppId,10), Users=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Events desc
APPLICATION
index=salesforce sourcetype="sfdc:eventloginfile" (EVENT_TYPE="API" OR EVENT_TYPE="RestApi" OR EVENT_TYPE="BulkApi") (SOURCE_IP="138.226.246.94" OR SOURCE_IP="212.86.125.24" OR SOURCE_IP="213.111.148.90" OR SOURCE_IP="94.154.32.160" OR CLIENT_IP="138.226.246.94" OR CLIENT_IP="212.86.125.24" OR CLIENT_IP="213.111.148.90" OR CLIENT_IP="94.154.32.160")
| stats count AS ApiCalls, values(URI) AS Endpoints, values(CONNECTED_APP_ID) AS ConnectedAppId, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen by USER_ID, SOURCE_IP, CLIENT_IP
| sort - ApiCalls
First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces a Connected App ID that has never been observed in the tenant baseline suddenly issuing API calls or report exports — the pattern left by ShinyHunters' vishing-driven OAuth consent to a malicious app disguised as the legitimate Salesforce Data Loader. Catches consent-phishing even when the source IP is not a known IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's own ConnectedAppId extraction (RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID / ConnectedAppId, code Block 1) but replaces the non-schema UncommonForUser flag with a 30-day first-seen anti-join — a newly-consented app doing bulk API/export is exactly the malicious 'Data Loader' behaviour Microsoft describes. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new integration onboarded by IT during the lookback window (e.g. a sanctioned analytics or backup app)
  • Salesforce Data Loader genuinely used by an admin for a one-off migration
  • Connected App re-registered with a new ID after a secret rotation
  • Sandbox-to-prod app promotion generating a first-seen ID
Suppression filter
| where UAs has_any ("python","Salesforce-","Bulk API","axios","node-fetch","Go-http-client") or Events > 500  // narrow to automated bulk-access user-agents / high volume
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ConnectedApp's granted OAuth scopes and the consenting user; check whether the consent event correlates with a help-desk/vishing report or an unusual admin session. 2) Contain: revoke the app's tokens, remove the Connected App, and force-reauth/reset the consenting user if a scope like api or full was granted. 3) Hunt: list every record type queried/exported by the app, cross-reference the five IOC IPs, and review other users who consented to the same app name across the tenant.
let Baseline = CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Application == "Salesforce"
    | extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
    | where isnotempty(ConnectedAppId)
    | distinct ConnectedAppId;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType in ("ApiTotalUsage","API Event","ReportExport")
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| where isnotempty(ConnectedAppId)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on ConnectedAppId
| summarize Events=count(), Users=dcount(AccountId), Actions=make_set(ActionType,5), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,5), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by ConnectedAppId
| order by Events desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Baseline = CloudAppEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Application == "Salesforce"
    | extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
    | where isnotempty(ConnectedAppId)
    | distinct ConnectedAppId;
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType in ("ApiTotalUsage","API Event","ReportExport")
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| where isnotempty(ConnectedAppId)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on ConnectedAppId
| summarize Events=count(), Users=dcount(AccountId), Actions=make_set(ActionType,5), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,5), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by ConnectedAppId
| order by Events desc
APPLICATION
index=salesforce sourcetype="sfdc:eventloginfile" earliest=-1d (EVENT_TYPE="API" OR EVENT_TYPE="RestApi" OR EVENT_TYPE="BulkApi" OR EVENT_TYPE="ReportExport") CONNECTED_APP_ID=*
| stats count AS Events, dc(USER_ID) AS Users, values(SOURCE_IP) AS SourceIps, values(EVENT_TYPE) AS Actions, min(_time) AS firstSeen by CONNECTED_APP_ID
| search NOT [ search index=salesforce sourcetype="sfdc:eventloginfile" earliest=-30d latest=-1d CONNECTED_APP_ID=* | stats count by CONNECTED_APP_ID | fields CONNECTED_APP_ID ]
| sort - Events
Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Salesforce user identity exporting reports at a volume far above normal, the mass-exfiltration step Microsoft observed across all three ShinyHunters intrusion paths (accounts, contacts, and service-case data pulled at scale). Pivots on Salesforce report-export events rather than authentication, which the actors evade. Rationale: Built directly on the article's ReportExport code (Block 2, RawEventData.USER_ID) and Microsoft's 'Possible Salesforce scraping activity' coverage; a per-hour export burst is the concrete exfiltration signal for accounts/contacts/case data the actors bulk-queried. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/shinyhunters-and-unc6395-inside-the-salesforce-and-salesloft-breaches
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quarterly business-review or finance close where an analyst legitimately exports many reports
  • A scheduled BI/ETL service account performing routine bulk report pulls
  • Data-migration or Salesforce backup job running as a user identity
  • Sales-ops power user building a large territory dataset
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc","integration","backup","etl") and UAs has_any ("Salesforce Reporting","DataLoader","Informatica"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SalesforceUserId is a human, an integration/service account, or a hijacked session; compare the export IPs/user-agents against the five IOC IPs and the user's normal geo. 2) Contain: suspend the Salesforce session/user and revoke associated OAuth grants; enable/verify Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring transaction security to block further exports. 3) Hunt: enumerate the specific reports/objects exported, assess data sensitivity, and pivot to Connected-App attribution to see if the exports rode a compromised integration token.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType == "ReportExport"
| extend SalesforceUserId = tostring(RawEventData.USER_ID)
| summarize Exports=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), AccountObjectId, AccountId, AccountDisplayName, SalesforceUserId
| where Exports > 50   // 50 exports/hr >> typical per-user report cadence; empirical bulk-exfil threshold
| order by Exports desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType == "ReportExport"
| extend SalesforceUserId = tostring(RawEventData.USER_ID)
| summarize Exports=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), AccountObjectId, AccountId, AccountDisplayName, SalesforceUserId
| where Exports > 50   // 50 exports/hr >> typical per-user report cadence; empirical bulk-exfil threshold
| order by Exports desc
WEB
index=salesforce sourcetype="sfdc:eventloginfile" EVENT_TYPE="ReportExport"
| bucket _time span=1h
| stats count AS Exports, values(SOURCE_IP) AS SourceIps, values(CLIENT_IP) AS ClientIps, values(USER_AGENT) AS UserAgents by _time, USER_ID
| where Exports > 50
| sort - Exports
Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts unauthenticated guest-user Salesforce activity from IOC IP 103.75.11.78 (Microsoft: targeting the Aura framework via guest access, 19–22 June), where chained Aura/GraphQL requests circumvented record-retrieval limits to scrape data far beyond normal guest scope. Targets the misconfigured-guest-access intrusion path. Rationale: Anchors on the single IOC IP Microsoft attributes specifically to Aura-framework guest-access data theft (Table 2, 19–22 June window) and surfaces the guest/USER_TYPE context — a fixed IP tied to a named intrusion path makes this alerting-grade and distinct from the integration-IP UC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1213 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vulnerability scanner or bug-bounty researcher probing the org's Experience Cloud / Aura endpoints from that IP after IOC publication
  • Legitimate high-volume anonymous community-portal browsing sharing the IP via CGNAT
  • IR/pentest engagement replaying the Aura request chain for validation
  • Third-party uptime monitor hitting public community pages
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the activity is guest/unauthenticated (USER_TYPE) and enumerate the Aura/GraphQL endpoints and objects returned; determine which guest-exposed records were reachable. 2) Contain: tighten guest-user object/field permissions and sharing rules on the affected Experience Cloud site, disable unauthenticated Aura endpoints not required, and block the IP. 3) Hunt: review all guest-user activity across community sites for chained Aura/GraphQL scraping patterns and abnormally large result sets, and check for the same IP against the other Salesforce intrusion paths.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress == "103.75.11.78"
| extend UserType = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.USER_TYPE, RawEventData.UserType))
| summarize Requests=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,15), UserTypes=make_set(UserType,5), Accounts=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Requests desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress == "103.75.11.78"
| extend UserType = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.USER_TYPE, RawEventData.UserType))
| summarize Requests=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,15), UserTypes=make_set(UserType,5), Accounts=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Requests desc
APPLICATION
index=salesforce sourcetype="sfdc:eventloginfile" (SOURCE_IP="103.75.11.78" OR CLIENT_IP="103.75.11.78")
| stats count AS Requests, values(EVENT_TYPE) AS EventTypes, values(URI) AS Endpoints, values(USER_TYPE) AS UserTypes, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen by USER_ID, SOURCE_IP
| sort - Requests
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-61667: DIRAC is vulnerable to RCE in FileCatalog DatasetManager via SQL injection + eval

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-07-13 6 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

DIRAC is vulnerable to RCE in FileCatalog DatasetManager via SQL injection + eval

CVEsCVE-2026-61667
ATT&CKT1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SQL injection in DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset datasets parameter (CVE-2026-61667) · [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog python service spawns shell/interpreter child (eval RCE, CVE-2026-61667) · [LLM] Authenticated DIRAC identity issuing anomalous/first-seen injected FileCatalog calls (CVE-2026-61667 privesc)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-RCE read of dirac.cfg / proxy / token store by DIRAC service context (CVE-2026-61667) · [LLM] DIRAC dirac.cfg exfiltration to external host post-RCE (CVE-2026-61667)
SQL injection in DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset datasets parameter (CVE-2026-61667) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts DIRAC FileCatalog / DatasetManager application logs for SQL-injection metacharacters and Python eval() RCE markers appearing in the user-controlled `datasets` argument of checkDataset. Because the injected SQL result is passed straight to eval(), attacker payloads carry Python primitives (__import__, os.system, subprocess) that never appear in a legitimate dataset name. Rationale: The advisory states checkDataset passes its `datasets` argument unescaped into an f-string SQL query and the result reaches eval; a real dataset name never contains UNION SELECT or Python primitives like __import__/os.system, so these tokens in FileCatalog log lines are high-fidelity. Defender/Falcon left empty: DIRAC application-layer DB query text is not shipped to endpoint EDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://github.com/DIRACGrid/DIRAC/blob/f7e0a3ac153315030fb3520e8ca747f013758967/src/DIRAC/DataManagementSystem/DB/FileCatalogComponents/DatasetManager/DatasetManager.py • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-61667
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pentest / vulnerability scan against the FileCatalog endpoint replaying the PoC
  • Legitimate dataset names that coincidentally contain the substring 'OR' with surrounding spaces
  • DIRAC developers running unit/integration tests against DatasetManager
  • Log lines echoing a previously-blocked payload during patch validation
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "integration_test" and SyslogMessage !has "pytest"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full SyslogMessage and the source IP / proxy DN that issued the checkDataset call; confirm the DIRAC version is < 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 2) Contain: block the offending client certificate/proxy, and if patch is not yet applied, take the FileCatalog service offline or firewall it to trusted hosts. 3) Hunt: pivot to the DIRAC host for child-process spawns from the FileCatalog python service (UC2) and reads of dirac.cfg / proxy store (UC4) in the minutes after this log line.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "dirac" or SyslogMessage has_any ("FileCatalog", "DatasetManager", "checkDataset")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION SELECT", "union select", "' OR ", "OR 1=1", " -- ", "__import__", "os.system", "subprocess", "__builtins__", "compile(", "eval(")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog ("FileCatalog" OR "DatasetManager" OR "checkDataset") AND ("UNION SELECT" OR "__import__" OR "os.system" OR "subprocess" OR "__builtins__" OR "OR 1=1")
APPLICATION
index=dirac (source=*FileCatalog* OR source=*DatasetManager* OR sourcetype=dirac*) ("UNION SELECT" OR "__import__" OR "os.system" OR "subprocess" OR "__builtins__" OR "OR 1=1" OR "' OR " OR "compile(") | table _time host source sourcetype _raw | sort - _time
DIRAC FileCatalog python service spawns shell/interpreter child (eval RCE, CVE-2026-61667) AIExploitation High
Detects the DIRAC FileCatalog / DatasetManager service (a python Tornado/DISET process) spawning a shell, network tool, or interpreter — the observable footprint of eval() executing attacker-controlled code returned from the injected SQL query. A catalog service has no legitimate reason to fork sh/bash/curl. Rationale: The advisory's core sink is eval() on SQLi-controlled data inside DatasetManager; the parent process command line carries the DIRAC component name (e.g. DataManagement/FileCatalog), so a shell/interpreter child of that exact python service is a near-zero-baseline RCE signal. Falcon/Datadog can only key on parent=python + shell child (parent cmdline enrichment recommended), hence the FP note. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://github.com/DIRACGrid/DIRAC/blob/f7e0a3ac153315030fb3520e8ca747f013758967/src/DIRAC/DataManagementSystem/DB/FileCatalogComponents/DatasetManager/DatasetManager.py
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin invoking a DIRAC management CLI from the same python venv that shells out for diagnostics
  • DIRAC installation/upgrade scripts (dirac-install) shelling out during deployment
  • Monitoring agents (Nagios/Prometheus exporters) launched under the DIRAC service tree
  • Legitimate DIRAC agents that call external tools (e.g. gfal/xrdcp) — narrow parent filter to FileCatalog/DatasetManager to exclude
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-install", "dirac-configure", "dirac-admin") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and its SHA256; correlate the timestamp with UC1 FileCatalog SQLi log lines on the same host to confirm the eval vector. 2) Contain: kill the child process tree, isolate the DIRAC host from the network, and revoke/rotate the DB credentials in dirac.cfg (assume compromised). 3) Hunt: search for follow-on reads of dirac.cfg and proxy/token stores (UC4) and outbound egress from the DIRAC service context (UC5); check local DIRAC logs for tampering/deletion.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python"

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "perl", "python")

Authenticated DIRAC identity issuing anomalous/first-seen injected FileCatalog calls (CVE-2026-61667 privesc) AIExploitation Medium
Attributes CVE-2026-61667 exploitation to an authenticated DIRAC identity by flagging a proxy/DN that issues checkDataset calls carrying SQLi/eval markers for the first time versus a 30-day baseline. The advisory requires an authenticated (low-privilege) user, so surfacing which normal account suddenly performs injected catalog operations is the privilege-escalation pivot. Rationale: The advisory stresses 'any authenticated user' as the prerequisite; extracting the DN/user from the FileCatalog log line and anti-joining against a 30-day baseline isolates the specific low-priv identity that pivoted to injection, which is the privesc attribution the other content-only UCs miss. Defender/Falcon empty: DIRAC identity+app correlation lives in application/auth logs, not endpoint EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://github.com/DIRACGrid/DIRAC/blob/f7e0a3ac153315030fb3520e8ca747f013758967/src/DIRAC/DataManagementSystem/Service/FileCatalogHandler.py
ATT&CKT1078 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A new legitimate DIRAC user whose first-ever catalog queries happen to contain flagged substrings
  • Security team running an authorized exploitation test under a test proxy
  • Log-parsing regex failing to extract the DN (empty DiracUser) on a non-standard log format
  • Batch reprocessing job replaying historical catalog operations after a schema migration
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DiracUser/DN and its normal role; confirm it is a low-privilege account per the advisory's 'authenticated user' prerequisite. 2) Contain: revoke that user's proxy/token, disable the account, and rotate any shared service proxies exported from the host. 3) Hunt: correlate the account's source IP across the auth log, and check the DIRAC host for eval-driven process spawns (UC2) and credential-store reads (UC4) tied to the same session.
let Baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "checkDataset"
    | extend DiracUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:user|DN|owner)[=:\s]+([^\s,;]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(DiracUser)
    | summarize by DiracUser;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "checkDataset"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION SELECT", "__import__", "os.system", "subprocess", "OR 1=1", " -- ")
| extend DiracUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:user|DN|owner)[=:\s]+([^\s,;]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DiracUser
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, DiracUser, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-RCE read of dirac.cfg / proxy / token store by DIRAC service context (CVE-2026-61667) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects reading of the DIRAC secrets (dirac.cfg holding DB passwords, and the proxy/token store) by a shell, network tool, or interpreter descended from the compromised FileCatalog service. The advisory explicitly names dirac.cfg and stored proxies/tokens as the post-exploitation loot. Rationale: The advisory names dirac.cfg (DB passwords) and stored proxies/tokens as the exfil targets; the DIRAC service reads dirac.cfg at startup, so keying on a shell/network-tool child (not the python service itself) reading these paths avoids the startup baseline while catching hands-on-keyboard credential theft. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6

DIRAC dirac.cfg exfiltration to external host post-RCE (CVE-2026-61667) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects staging of dirac.cfg for exfiltration — either a single curl/scp/python command that reads dirac.cfg and points at an external destination, or (Defender/Sentinel) a dirac.cfg read followed within 10 minutes by outbound egress from the same host. Targets the advisory's stated goal of stealing DB passwords and proxies off the box. Rationale: The advisory states the attacker reads dirac.cfg to obtain DB passwords and exports proxies/tokens; a curl/scp/python command that both references dirac.cfg and carries an external URL/host is a single-event exfil primitive, while Defender/Sentinel add the temporal file-read-then-egress correlation for tooling that stages then transfers separately. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Admin uploading dirac.cfg to a support/pastebin for troubleshooting
  • Backup agent transferring /opt/dirac/etc to an internal backup target (filter internal destinations)
  • Configuration-management pull of dirac.cfg over HTTPS from an internal repo
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168." or RemoteIP startswith "172.16.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve RemoteIP/Url — is the destination an internal DIRAC/backup host or an unknown external IP? Grab the full command line. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, and rotate every credential in dirac.cfg plus all exported proxies/tokens (assume exfiltrated). 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination IP across the estate, review DIRAC local logs for deletion/tampering (the advisory notes attackers can wipe log evidence), and confirm patch to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10.
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

    | where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FileCatalog", "DatasetManager") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash")
    | project CfgTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "curl", "wget", "scp", "sftp", "sh", "bash", "nc", "ncat")
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, EgressTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by CfgTime desc
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
    | project CfgTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, CfgCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, EgressTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, CfgCmd, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by CfgTime desc

CrashStealer notarized dropper 'veltod' / Werkbit.app execution (Gatekeeper bypass) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the Apple-notarized CrashStealer dropper — the 'veltod' Mach-O inside 'Werkbit.app' signed by Developer ID 'Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV)', bundle id dev.golove.velto. This is the article's core defense-evasion pivot: a notarized/right-clicked app that clears Gatekeeper before fetching the stealer payload. Rationale: Pins on the exact article strings 'veltod' and 'Werkbit.app' (corroborated by Jamf and SecurityAffairs); both are unique, non-Apple names so any hit is high-fidelity even though Apple has since revoked the Developer ID. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-crashstealer-malware-poses-as-apple-crash-reporting-tool/

1) Triage: pull the process's code-signing authority and team ID — confirm Developer ID 'Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV)' / bundle dev.golove.velto and capture the SHA256 and origin DMG (werkbit.io). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the veltod/CrashReporter process tree, and quarantine the .app + any /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for outbound connections to 179.43.166.242 / endpoint-api-v1.com and for a new ~/Library/LaunchAgents plist to catch persistence and exfil.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "veltod" or FolderPath has "Werkbit.app" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Werkbit.app"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer dropper staging: veltod → curl/shell fetch from GitHub 'mgothiclove' to /tmp AIDelivery High
Hunts the CrashStealer delivery chain: the 'veltod' dropper contacting GitHub repo mgothiclove (sys.cache) to extract a curl command, pulling a shell-script downloader, and staging the next-stage 'CrashReporter.dmg' into /tmp. Targets the parent→child (veltod → curl/sh) plus the /tmp payload write. Rationale: Chains the article's concrete parent (veltod), the GitHub repo mgothiclove (corroborated as mgothiclove/pkeys by Jamf), the sys.cache/CrashReporter.dmg filenames and the /tmp staging directory — a specific multi-string combination unlikely outside this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scripts that curl release artifacts from GitHub and write to /tmp (verify parent is not veltod)
  • macOS app updaters staging .dmg files in /tmp
  • Homebrew/CI pipelines invoking curl+bash one-liners
  • Security tooling downloading definitions to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("brew","softwareupdated") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent binary is veltod/Werkbit.app and capture the full curl URL and the staged /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the veltod→curl→sh chain, quarantine /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg and the DMG. 3) Hunt: check the same host and org for GitHub pulls from mgothiclove, connections to endpoint-api-v1.com/179.43.166.242, and any new LaunchAgent plist referencing /tmp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "veltod" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Werkbit.app"
| where FileName in~ ("curl","sh","bash","zsh")
     or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("github.com/mgothiclove","mgothiclove","sys.cache","CrashReporter.dmg","endpoint-api-v1.com","/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer keychain/browser/wallet harvesting into ZIP archive AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CrashStealer's collection stage: the veltod/CrashReporter process reading the login keychain, Chromium-family browser credential/cookie stores, crypto-wallet extensions and password-manager data, then packaging them into a ZIP for exfil. Article-specific because the reader process is the malware, not a browser. Rationale: Ties the malware processes (veltod/CrashReporter/Werkbit.app) to the exact credential-store paths the article enumerates (keychain, Chromium creds/cookies, ~80 wallet extensions, 14 password managers) plus the ZIP packaging step — reader-process identity is what makes it non-generic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-password-theft/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1555.003 T1005 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate macOS backup software (e.g. Time Machine helpers) reading keychain/browser dirs — but not under a veltod/CrashReporter parent
  • A password-manager's own updater touching its data dir
  • Browser sync writing Login Data (initiating process would be the browser, filtered out)
  • Analyst tooling zipping a user profile for forensics
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","Google Chrome Helper","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","1Password 7","1Password","Bitwarden")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is veltod/CrashReporter (not the browser itself) and list which stores were read plus the ZIP output path. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, quarantine the ZIP before it egresses, and force-rotate the user's keychain/browser/wallet/password-manager credentials. 3) Hunt: look for the subsequent libcurl POST to 179.43.166.242/endpoint-api-v1.com and confirm whether the ZIP left the host.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Werkbit.app"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/Keychains","login.keychain","/Application Support/Google/Chrome","/Application Support/BraveSoftware","/Application Support/Microsoft Edge","/Application Support/com.operasoftware","Login Data","/Library/Cookies","MetaMask","Phantom","1Password","Bitwarden","LastPass")
    or (FileName endswith ".zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,

| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer LaunchAgent persistence plist written by dropper/payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CrashStealer establishing persistence by writing a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist while the writing process is the veltod dropper or CrashReporter payload (which persists by copying and re-signing itself). Narrow because it keys on the malware process as the plist author. Rationale: Combines the article's stated LaunchAgent persistence with the specific author processes (veltod/CrashReporter/Werkbit.app) so it fires only when the malware writes autostart, not on the thousands of legitimate LaunchAgent plists that exist. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-crashstealer-malware-poses-as-apple-crash-reporting-tool/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1547.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately named binary writing its own LaunchAgent (verify signer/hash)
  • EDR restore replaying a quarantined plist
  • Sanctioned lab detonation of the sample
  • Admin manually re-registering a launch agent during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written plist — capture its Label, ProgramArguments path (likely /tmp or a re-signed copy) and RunAtLoad flag. 2) Contain: isolate host, unload/remove the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout), delete the referenced binary and quarantine the plist. 3) Hunt: enumerate all ~/Library/LaunchAgents + /Library/LaunchDaemons org-wide for plists referencing /tmp or the CrashReporter binary, and check for C2 egress to 179.43.166.242.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Werkbit.app"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")

CrashStealer C2 / exfil egress to 179.43.166.242 and campaign domains AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CrashStealer's libcurl exfiltration and C2: outbound connections to the hardcoded server 179.43.166.242 (present as an ATS exception in the sample's Info.plist) or the campaign domains (werkbit.io, endpoint-api-v1.com, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io, icky-lyrical.com), especially from the malware process rather than a browser. Rationale: 179.43.166.242 is the article's hardcoded exfil endpoint (corroborated by Jamf/SecurityAffairs as an Info.plist ATS exception) and the six campaign domains come from the vendor IOC bundle — fixed indicators give a low-FP alerting signal; excluding browser processes reinforces that a stealer, not the user, is beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox in the org resolving/probing the IOC domains
  • A security researcher detonating the sample and generating C2 traffic
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse — 179.43.166.242 later hosting a benign service (verify with passive DNS)
  • Proxy/DNS sinkhole appliance logging the domain as it blocks it
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "deny"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the source host and confirm it is veltod/CrashReporter (not a browser) and whether a ZIP was uploaded. 2) Contain: block 179.43.166.242 and the six domains at firewall/DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the malware process. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for any prior connection to these IOCs and for the upstream chain (Werkbit.app execution, GitHub mgothiclove pulls, LaunchAgent persistence); rotate credentials on any host that beaconed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "179.43.166.242"
     or RemoteUrl has_any ("werkbit.io","endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","icky-lyrical.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("com.apple.WebKit.Networking","Safari","Google Chrome Helper","firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "179.43.166.242"
     or DestinationHostName has_any ("werkbit.io","endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","icky-lyrical.com")
     or RequestURL has_any ("werkbit.io","endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","icky-lyrical.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-45579: DIRAC is vulnerable to RCE in RequestManager due to eval on untrusted input

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-07-13 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

DIRAC is vulnerable to RCE in RequestManager due to eval on untrusted input

CVEsCVE-2026-45579
ATT&CKT1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft)
DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload executing: the DIRAC RequestManager service (a Python DB-facing handler launched via dirac-service/dirac-tornado as ReqManager/TornadoReqManager) spawning /bin/sh, bash or a recon/egress tool. The eval() on the unrecognised groupingAttribute walks back to the os module, so successful exploitation manifests as this DB service forking a shell — something ReqManager never does legitimately (unlike RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a ProcessPool). Rationale: Anchored on the ReqManager/ReqManagerHandler/dirac-service parent identity (DIRAC docs: ReqManager is the DB-facing handler that never shells out) combined with any shell/recon/egress child — the exact tree the eval()->os.* chain from the advisory produces. Parent token deliberately excludes RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a legitimate ProcessPool. Datadog/Falcon left empty: their provided auditd/ProcessRollup2 schemas expose no parent command line to key the DIRAC-service parent on (only ParentBaseFileName='python', too generic). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x • https://dirac.diracgrid.org/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/Systems/RequestManagement/rmsComponents.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator running diagnostic shell commands under the runit/supervisor process tree during service troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint/init wrapper spawning a shell during a dirac-service (re)start
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet/Salt) restarting dirac-tornado and running post-restart health-check shell hooks
  • Site monitoring probes (monit/nagios) that shell out from the service supervisor
  • A local health-check script using curl/nc to poll the ReqManager port on service start
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "healthcheck" and ChildCmd !has "/opt/dirac/pro/versions" and ChildCmd !has "runsvdir"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; correlate against the ReqManager log for the exception traceback the advisory says the exploit leaves (NameError/AttributeError referencing 'Request.' or dunder strings such as __class__/__globals__/__builtins__), and identify the authenticated user whose RPC to getRequestCountersWeb preceded it. 2) Contain: isolate the DIRAC host, rotate all secrets in dirac.cfg (database passwords) and revoke every stored proxy/token, then upgrade DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: search the same host for reads of dirac.cfg by non-DIRAC processes, outbound egress from the service, and truncation/deletion of the RequestManager log (evidence removal noted in the advisory).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","id","whoami","hostname","uname","cat","base64","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/id","/whoami","/hostname","/uname","/cat","/base64","/chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-theft step the advisory describes: after the eval() RCE, the attacker reads the local dirac.cfg to harvest database passwords and export stored proxies/tokens. Keys on a read/exfil utility (cat, grep, base64, curl, etc.) whose own command line references dirac.cfg — excluding the Python DIRAC service that carries dirac.cfg as a legitimate --cfg argument. Rationale: Keys on dirac.cfg (the file the advisory names as holding DB passwords and gating proxy/token export) appearing in the command line of a read/exfil utility rather than the Python service. The reader-binary allowlist excludes the legitimate DIRAC process, which carries dirac.cfg as a --cfg argument — so any cat/grep/base64/curl of dirac.cfg is anomalous. Portable across all process-telemetry platforms because it keys on the executing process's own command line. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator manually running cat/grep on dirac.cfg during troubleshooting over SSH
  • Backup jobs (tar/rsync driven via cat) reading the DIRAC etc/ directory
  • Config-management tooling templating or diffing dirac.cfg on each run
  • Monitoring/inventory scripts grepping dirac.cfg for a version or option value
  • Site install/upgrade scripts copying dirac.cfg with scp/curl to a new node
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of the reader process — if it descends from the DIRAC service (dirac-service/dirac-tornado/ReqManager) rather than an interactive admin shell, treat as confirmed exploitation; check whether the command pipes to base64/curl/nc (exfil) and whether stored proxy/token files were touched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg and revoke all stored user proxies and tokens, and patch DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: pivot on the authenticated user who called getRequestCountersWeb, review the ReqManager log for the eval exception traceback, and look for outbound transfers of dirac.cfg / proxy material and any subsequent log truncation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","less","more","head","tail","base64","od","strings","xxd","curl","wget","scp","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/cat","/grep","/egrep","/less","/more","/head","/tail","/base64","/od","/strings","/xxd","/curl","/wget","/scp","/nc","/ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google and Microsoft Pull ModHeader With 1.6 Million Installs After Dormant Collector Found

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google and Microsoft have pulled ModHeader, a popular header-editing extension with roughly 1.6 million installs across Chrome and Edge, after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector built into its official store version. The collector was dormant. An empty allow-list kept it switched off, and no proof has emerged that it ever gathered or sent a single browsing domain. The

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution and network connections to the two domains hardwired into the trojanised ModHeader extension: extensions-hub.com (pinged on install/update/uninstall, confirmed active) and api.stanfordstudies.com (the dormant daily browsing-history exfil endpoint). Because the browser process itself makes the call, the connection is attributed to chrome.exe/msedge.exe. Rationale: Both domains are named directly in the article and corroborated by Yunus Aydın and HackIndex teardowns; extensions-hub.com fires on every install/update/uninstall (confirmed active), making this a reliable trip-wire even though the browsing-history exfil path is gated off. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://hackindex.io/research/modheader-malware-chrome-spyware • https://gbhackers.com/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000-users/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-registered but similarly-named advertising domain sharing the extensions-hub.com string in a subdomain
  • Security researchers or the SOC intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domains for verdict lookups
  • A proxy/DNS-security appliance's own IOC-testing beacon
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe) and check whether the host has the ModHeader extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj on disk (see the extension-inventory UC). 2) CONTAIN: Block stanfordstudies.com and extensions-hub.com at DNS and proxy; push removal of the ModHeader extension and verify no managed-extension policy / profile-sync will reinstall it. 3) HUNT: If the host also beaconed to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log, treat the collector as activated — pull proxy logs for the POST body size and rotate any API keys / bearer tokens / session cookies the user pasted into ModHeader's header history.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("stanfordstudies.com", "extensions-hub.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("stanfordstudies.com", "extensions-hub.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host AIInstallation High
Inventories hosts where the pulled ModHeader extension is (or was) installed by matching its Chrome/Edge Web Store extension ID in the on-disk extension directory. This finds the affected population regardless of whether the dormant collector ever fired, so you can drive removal and secret-rotation. Rationale: The extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj is the single most durable IOC in the article — it is fixed, unique to the pulled build, and appears in the browser's on-disk extension directory whether or not the collector activated, giving a clean affected-host inventory. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/google-and-microsoft-pull-modheader.html • https://hackindex.io/research/modheader-malware-chrome-spyware • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/modheader-malware/
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • This ID is unique to the pulled ModHeader build, so true FPs are near-zero; a benign hit would be a security team staging the sample for analysis
  • Backup/EDR agents copying an existing extension directory during imaging (path still confirms exposure)
  • A forensic image being mounted/scanned on an analyst workstation
  • Roaming-profile sync replaying the folder onto a new host after the extension was already removed
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the extension directory is live (not an archived/backup copy) and identify the browser profile owner. 2) CONTAIN: Force-remove the extension from Chrome and Edge, then verify no ExtensionInstallForcelist GPO/Intune policy or profile-sync will reinstall it; uninstalling clears its stored data. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these hosts against the collector-callback UC; for any user who used ModHeader's header-history feature, rotate API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies, since full HTTP headers were stored on disk in plaintext.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=count(), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=count(), SamplePath=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log AIActions on Objectives High
Targets the collector's activated exfiltration path specifically: an HTTP POST to api.stanfordstudies.com with the URI /app/log, which uploads the encrypted domain list plus device fingerprint before wiping the local copy. Requires web-proxy/gateway telemetry that captures URI and method, so it distinguishes real exfil from the dormant-state domain resolution. Rationale: The article and Yunus Aydın's teardown both name the exact upload target — a POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log carrying the encrypted domain list and fingerprint — so matching host+method+URI on proxy logs is a high-fidelity signal that the dormant collector has actually been switched on. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://cyberpress.org/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1082
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign traffic to an unrelated host that reuses the /app/log URI path on a different domain (host filter mitigates this)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample generating the POST intentionally
  • A DLP/CASB solution replaying the request for inspection
  • Threat-intel tooling probing the endpoint for a live-verdict check
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the POST targeted api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log from a browser process and note SentBytes — a non-trivial body means the encrypted domain list was uploaded. 2) CONTAIN: Sinkhole/block stanfordstudies.com at DNS and proxy, remove the ModHeader extension from the host, and isolate if body size indicates bulk upload. 3) HUNT: This confirms the allow-list was populated (collector active) — sweep all hosts with the extension ID for the same POST, and rotate every secret (API keys, bearer tokens, session cookies) the affected users pasted into ModHeader's header-history feature, which stored full HTTP headers in plaintext on disk.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where RequestMethod == "POST" or RequestURL has "/app/log"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
