Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance (Gentlemen network mapping) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Exposure scoping for Gentlemen-exploited initial-access CVEs
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task 'gentlemen*' / gentlemen_system creation · [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys / ThrottleBlood.sys vulnerable driver drop (CVE-2025-7771) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Gentlemen/SystemBC infrastructure IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windows event-log clearing via wevtutil (Gentlemen anti-forensics) · [LLM] Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic (Gentlemen pre-encryption) · [LLM] Rapid mass file modification by a single process (Gentlemen Go encryptor) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task 'gentlemen*' / gentlemen_system creation AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or execution of a Windows scheduled task whose name matches the article-specified 'gentlemen*' pattern (corroborated task names gentlemen_system and UpdateSystem, run as SYSTEM). This is the single most Gentlemen-specific execution/persistence artifact Unit 42 recommends alerting on. Rationale: Anchored on Unit 42's explicit recommendation to alert on scheduled tasks matching 'gentlemen*', enriched with the concrete task names gentlemen_system/UpdateSystem confirmed by Microsoft Threat Intelligence's Storm-2697 write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/ransomware-uses-system-scheduled-task/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A homegrown IT tool or script that legitimately contains the substring 'UpdateSystem' in a task name
  • Security team creating a detection/EICAR test task named to mimic the threat
  • Backup/patch automation that names tasks with 'System' plus operator typo matching pattern
  • Threat-hunt or purple-team exercise deliberately deploying the named task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "gentlemen")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks command line and the parent process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) — a task named gentlemen_system running as SYSTEM spawned by a non-admin/temp binary is a confirmed hit. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the malicious task (schtasks /delete), and snapshot the referenced executable for IR before it self-propagates over SMB. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same task name, for ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys driver drops, and for wevtutil log-clearing on the same DeviceId within the prior hour.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen" or ProcessCommandLine has "UpdateSystem"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/run","/change","/delete")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4698
| where EventData has "gentlemen" or EventData has "UpdateSystem"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys / ThrottleBlood.sys vulnerable driver drop (CVE-2025-7771) AIInstallation High
Hunts the drop/load of the Gentlemen EDR-killer's vulnerable driver ThrottleStop.sys (renamed ThrottleBlood.sys by the actor) abused via CVE-2025-7771 to terminate 400+ security processes. Targets the file/image artifact of the BYOVD stage rather than a generic driver-load rule. Rationale: Uses the article's named EDR-killer framework (GentleKiller) and CVE-2025-7771, with the specific driver filenames ThrottleStop.sys and its actor-renamed variant ThrottleBlood.sys confirmed by Trend Micro and ESET research. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ThrottleStop CPU-tuning utility installed by an overclocking enthusiast on an engineering workstation
  • Vendor OEM power-management package bundling the genuine ThrottleStop driver
  • Security researcher analyzing the driver in a sandbox VM that reports to production tenant
  • BYOVD-blocklist testing by the endpoint team
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("throttlestop.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Program Files\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .sys path and hash against the article/Microsoft blocklist; a drop into %Temp%/%ProgramData% or a rename to ThrottleBlood.sys is malicious regardless of signature (the driver itself is signed). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash, and verify Defender/EDR tamper-protection wasn't disabled — GentleKiller kills 400+ security processes. 3) Hunt: check for the gentlemen* scheduled task, wevtutil log clears, and any period where EDR heartbeat went silent on this host.
union
(DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FileName in~ ("ThrottleStop.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionKind="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FileName in~ ("ThrottleStop.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionKind="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has "ThrottleStop" or ServiceFileName has "ThrottleBlood"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows event-log clearing via wevtutil (Gentlemen anti-forensics) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts wevtutil.exe clearing the Security, System, or Application logs — the article-recommended behavioral alert and a corroborated Gentlemen anti-forensics step performed during encryption to destroy audit trails. Rationale: Directly implements Unit 42's 'behavioral alerts for systems executing wevtutil to clear Security/System logs' recommendation; Huntress/Microsoft confirm Gentlemen clears System, Application, and Security logs during its run. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing verbose logs during troubleshooting
  • Log-rotation or forwarding scripts that clear channels after archival
  • Golden-image / MDT build process wiping logs before sysprep
  • SIEM onboarding runbook that clears legacy local logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\CCM\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and user — wevtutil clearing Security logs from a non-interactive/SYSTEM ransomware parent, or clustered across many hosts, is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate affected hosts and preserve/forward any surviving EVTX and centralized copies immediately (local logs are already gone). 3) Hunt: correlate with EID 1102 (audit log cleared), the gentlemen* task, and shadow-copy deletion in the same window to confirm the encryption sequence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" cl ","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System","Application")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wevtutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (" cl ","clear-log")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Security","System","Application")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic (Gentlemen pre-encryption) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts destruction of Volume Shadow Copies through vssadmin delete shadows or wmic shadowcopy delete — the article-recommended Impact-phase behavioral alert that immediately precedes Gentlemen's Go-based encryption to block recovery. Rationale: Implements the article's explicit Impact recommendation to alert on vssadmin and wmic Volume Shadow Copy deletion, a documented pre-encryption step in the Gentlemen playbook. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/other backup software pruning snapshots during pre-job cleanup
  • Sysadmin manually clearing shadow storage to free disk
  • Windows Update/DISM servicing operations managing snapshots
  • VDI or imaging automation deleting shadows before recompose
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","vsnapvss.exe","dismhost.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the initiating process — a ransomware binary or SYSTEM scheduled task spawning vssadmin is a confirmed pre-encryption hit, whereas veeam.backup.shell.exe/services.exe is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host NOW; shadow deletion means encryption is imminent or underway — kill the parent process and pull network. 3) Hunt: look for the mass-file-encryption pattern, gentlemen* task, and wevtutil clears on the same and neighboring hosts (self-propagating Go encryptor spreads over SMB).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows")
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete shadows")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gentlemen Ransomware Shadow Copy Deletion

Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance (Gentlemen network mapping) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the named tool Gentlemen affiliates frequently use for internal network discovery and mapping prior to lateral movement and encryption. Rationale: Directly implements Unit 42's recommendation to monitor internal usage of Advanced IP Scanner, which they and other researchers name as a frequent Gentlemen recon tool. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hivepro.com/threat-advisory/the-gentlemen-ransomware-a-rapidly-scaling-raas-threat
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/network team legitimately inventorying subnets with Advanced IP Scanner
  • MSP technician running a portable scan during onboarding
  • Help-desk troubleshooting connectivity/asset discovery
  • Penetration test or authorized internal audit
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc-netscan") and DeviceName !in~ ("IT-JUMPBOX01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: is this a sanctioned admin host/user? Execution from a workstation, temp path, or non-IT account is suspicious. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and review what it scanned (arp/SMB fan-out) and any subsequent remote logons. 3) Hunt: pivot to SMB self-propagation, the gentlemen* task, and BYOVD driver drops on hosts the scanner touched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound C2 to Gentlemen/SystemBC infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint or firewall connections to the three IPs tied to Gentlemen affiliate C2/SystemBC infrastructure. Direct IOC match on network telemetry for the command-and-control phase the article flags around SystemBC signatures. Rationale: IOC-driven detection on the three campaign IPs pre-extracted from the article, mapped to the SystemBC C2 activity Unit 42 recommends monitoring; SystemBC's operational tie to Gentlemen is confirmed by second-source reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cybersecurity-insiders.com/gentlemen-ransomware-edr-killer-suite/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP has been re-allocated to a benign hosting tenant since the report (stale IOC)
  • Security researcher/sandbox in the tenant deliberately connecting to the C2 for analysis
  • Threat-intel platform actively probing the indicator
  • Shared cloud/VPS IP fronting unrelated legitimate services
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a non-browser/unknown binary beaconing to these IPs on a regular interval is high-fidelity SystemBC C2. 2) Contain: block the IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the beaconing process for IR. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts/firewall logs for the same IPs, decode any SystemBC-style traffic, and check the beaconing host for the gentlemen* task and EDR-killer driver.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DestinationIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rapid mass file modification by a single process (Gentlemen Go encryptor) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single process modifying/creating/renaming an anomalously high number of distinct files in a short window — the defining Impact behavior of Gentlemen's self-propagating Go encryptor. Threshold-based, filtered to non-machine actors and excluding known backup/sync tooling. Rationale: Implements reviewer-requested T1486 mass-encryption coverage grounded in the corroborated fact that Gentlemen is a self-propagating Go encryptor; threshold + single-process pivot + backup/sync exclusions keep it deployable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://darkatlas.io/blog/how-a-go-binary-locks-down-enterprise-networks-in-minutes-the-story-behind-gentlemen-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Commvault backup or restore job touching thousands of files
  • OneDrive/Dropbox/GDrive bulk sync after a large upload
  • Media/CAD/dev build process regenerating large asset trees
  • Disk-wide AV remediation or bulk decompression/extraction
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (".tmp","~")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating process path/hash and the file extensions being written — a temp/SYSTEM Go binary writing uniform new extensions across user data is ransomware. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, and disable the account; block SMB from the host to stop self-propagation. 3) Hunt: check for preceding shadow-copy deletion, wevtutil clears, and the gentlemen* task; identify patient-zero via the earliest encryption timestamp across hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","googledrivesync.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 500   // 500 distinct files / 5 min = well above interactive user editing
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "veeam" and ActingProcessName !has "OneDrive" and ActingProcessName !has "Dropbox"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 500   // 500 distinct files / 5 min encryption-rate threshold
| order by FileCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 -@Image:(*\OneDrive.exe OR *\Dropbox.exe OR *\veeam.backup.shell.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(onedrive|dropbox|veeam\.backup\.shell)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=FileCount))
| FileCount > 500
ENDPOINT

Exposure scoping for Gentlemen-exploited initial-access CVEs AIWeaponization High
Hunting query that surfaces devices in inventory still exposed to the five CVEs Unit 42 lists as actively exploited by Gentlemen for initial access and privilege escalation, so the SOC can prioritize patching of edge/VPN and driver-BYOVD exposure. Rationale: Turns Unit 42's explicit Initial Access and Privilege Escalation patch lists (CVE-2024-55591 FortiOS, CVE-2025-32433 Erlang/OTP SSH, CVE-2025-33073 SMB Client, CVE-2025-55182 React2Shell, CVE-2025-7771 ThrottleStop.sys) into an actionable exposure hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hivepro.com/threat-advisory/the-gentlemen-ransomware-a-rapidly-scaling-raas-threat
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reports a CVE on a device already compensating-controlled (WAF/segmentation)
  • Version detection false-positive where a backported vendor patch isn't recognized
  • End-of-life appliance flagged but scheduled for decommission
  • Duplicate device entries inflating the exposed count
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by internet-facing exposure (edge/VPN/SSH first — CVE-2024-55591, CVE-2025-32433, CVE-2025-33073) then endpoints for CVE-2025-7771. 2) Contain: emergency-patch or virtually-patch internet-facing devices and audit them for prior exploitation per the article's recommendation. 3) Hunt: on any exposed edge device, review auth/config logs and correlate with the endpoint detections in this set (BYOVD driver, gentlemen* task, SystemBC C2).

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API · [LLM] Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint
TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process invoking the tsdproxy management API on 127.0.0.1:8080 while injecting the leaked internal secret header x-tsdproxy-auth-token together with an attacker-controlled x-tsdproxy-id. These header names are unique to tsdproxy (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8) so their presence in a command line is a direct signature of the token-replay privilege-escalation exploit. Rationale: Keys on the two header names (x-tsdproxy-auth-token, x-tsdproxy-id) shown in the article's repro curl, paired with the fixed 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 management endpoint — all strings are unique to this vuln so an in-cmdline match is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked GitLab advisory mirror and CVEReports. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A maintainer or pentester validating the GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 fix by running the exact repro curl
  • Automated security-scanning tooling replaying the header to confirm the instance is patched
  • Internal red-team exercise reproducing the token-replay chain
  • A developer's shell-history / documentation snippet echoing the curl example that gets captured by process telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy") and ProcessCommandLine !has "scanner" and DeviceName !in~ ("pentest-lab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the initiating process/user; confirm the source process is a proxied backend (curl/wget/python/node/php) rather than the tsdproxy binary itself, and whether x-tsdproxy-id was set to a non-empty attacker value. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, rotate the tsdproxy internal token by restarting the service, and set identityHeaders: false pending upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review management API access logs (/api/v1/proxies, proxy restart/pause, webhook triggers) around the event, and check other backends sharing the tsdproxy host/network namespace for the same header string.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TSDProxy Internal Auth Token Replay to Management API
id: a1f4c2e0-8b3d-4c6a-9e21-7f0d5b3a9c11
description: Detects a process injecting the tsdproxy internal secret header (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) with a spoofed x-tsdproxy-id against the 127.0.0.1:8080 management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1550.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  token:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token'
      - 'x-tsdproxy-id'
  target:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '127.0.0.1:8080'
      - 'localhost:8080'
      - '/api/v1/'
  condition: token and target
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-auth-token* OR @process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-id*) (@process.command_line:*127.0.0.1:8080* OR @process.command_line:*localhost:8080* OR @process.command_line:*\/api\/v1\/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/x-tsdproxy-(auth-token|id)/i
| CommandLine=/(127\.0\.0\.1:8080|localhost:8080|\/api\/v1\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the tsdproxy management API path /api/v1/ on port 8080 arriving over loopback — the exact surface an attacker hits after stealing the forwarded token to enumerate proxies or issue admin operations (restart/pause/webhook). Because legitimate management access is Tailscale-fronted, loopback /api/v1 traffic bearing the tsdproxy identity headers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the concrete management endpoint (/api/v1/proxies) and port 8080 named in the article's repro, scoped to loopback where the token-replay must originate; captures the network-layer view the process-cmdline UC can miss when the attacker replays from a compiled backend rather than curl. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate tsdproxy self-calls to its own management API over loopback during normal operation
  • Local health-check or monitoring probe hitting /api/v1 on 8080
  • Admin using an SSH tunnel to reach the management UI, appearing as a loopback source
  • Container orchestration readiness/liveness probes against the management port
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication has_any ("curl","python","wget","go-http-client","node") or RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client user-agent (RequestClientApplication) and method — a curl/python UA or a POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/v1 from loopback is high-suspicion vs the tsdproxy service's own calls. 2) Contain: block external reachability to the management port, rotate the internal token via service restart, and disable identityHeaders. 3) Hunt: correlate with process telemetry (UC token-replay cmdline) on the same host and review whether proxy configs were enumerated or services restarted/paused via the API.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationPort == 8080
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/"
| where SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or DestinationIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog service:tsdproxy ("/api/v1/proxies" OR "/api/v1/")

Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080 AIExploitation Low
Surfaces a proxied backend process (curl/wget/python/node/php/shell) opening a connection to 127.0.0.1:8080 — the precondition the advisory calls out for token replay (backend must reach the management port on loopback). Pairs the leaked-token capture with the network reachability that turns it into management-API takeover. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's stated precondition ('attack requires the backend to reach 127.0.0.1:8080'); scoping to interpreter/CLI processes hitting loopback:8080 catches the reachability step even when the token itself isn't in a logged command line. Higher FP by nature, so hunting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backend app legitimately configured to call the management API over loopback (e.g., an admin dashboard on the same host)
  • Local monitoring/health-check scripts probing 8080
  • Another unrelated service also listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 (common dev port)
  • CI/CD or debug tooling on the host issuing loopback requests to 8080
  • Interpreter processes performing normal intra-host service calls unrelated to tsdproxy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm 8080 on the host is the tsdproxy management listener (not an unrelated dev service) and inspect the initiating process command line for the tsdproxy identity headers. 2) Contain: if the process is an untrusted/compromised backend, isolate the container, rotate the token via service restart, and set identityHeaders: false. 3) Hunt: pivot to process-cmdline telemetry for x-tsdproxy-auth-token on the same aid/host and review management API logs for enumeration or state-changing calls.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 8080
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","php","ruby","perl","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan Electron client spawns command interpreter (XSS-to-RCE via child_process) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payoff of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-44588: a stored XSS in an attribute-view cell executes in the SiYuan renderer (nodeIntegration:true) and calls require('child_process') to run native commands. A note-taking app spawning cmd/powershell/wscript is the concrete, article-specific outcome. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete RCE mechanism — Electron nodeIntegration renderer calling require('child_process') — pinned to the named parent binary SiYuan.exe. A knowledge/notes app spawning shells is near-zero baseline. Cross-checked against the SiYuan advisory, CVE-2026-39846 (same require('child_process').exec RCE pattern) and neighbor CVE-2026-44588. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50551
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. git-sync plugins invoking git via cmd.exe)
  • SiYuan updater/installer spawning a helper via cmd during version upgrade
  • A user-configured export/pandoc pipeline that SiYuan launches through a shell
  • Admin manually launching SiYuan from a script that reparents a console child
  • Security tooling that reparents processes and mislabels SiYuan.exe as the parent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\git.exe","pandoc","--update","siyuan-updater") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SiYuan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain — benign hits are git/pandoc/updater with recognizable args; malicious hits show base64/IEX/download-cradle or `calc`/reconnaissance commands and correlate to a recently opened note with an attribute-view. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan.exe process tree, and block outbound from any spawned child; preserve the offending data/storage/av/<avID>.json for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate the user's synced workspace peers (same account/sync target) for the same av JSON, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the spawned child reaching external hosts. Push SiYuan >= 3.7.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound network connection from a child process of SiYuan.exe (post-RCE C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts C2/exfil following CVE-2026-50551 exploitation: after the SiYuan renderer's XSS runs require('child_process'), the spawned interpreter/LOLBIN beacons out to attacker infrastructure. A shell whose parent is SiYuan.exe making a public egress is a high-signal post-exploitation pivot. Rationale: Pivots on the article's RCE mechanism into the network phase: a child of the named SiYuan.exe binary reaching a public host. Scoping to InitiatingProcessParentFileName == SiYuan.exe keeps FP near zero because SiYuan's own sync traffic originates from SiYuan.exe itself, not from a spawned shell. Sentinel/Datadog left blank — the listed Sentinel tables have no per-process egress with parent context, and Sysmon EID3 carries no ParentImage, so the parent scoping can't be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SiYuan git-sync plugin spawning git.exe that fetches over HTTPS
  • SiYuan update process invoking curl/bitsadmin to pull a release artifact
  • A user macro/export that shells out to a network-enabled CLI
  • certutil/curl launched by SiYuan for a legitimate asset download
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","b3log.org","liuyun.io") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\git.exe","--update","siyuan-updater"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve RemoteIP/RemoteUrl reputation and inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — download cradles, base64, or raw IP beacons are malicious; a known package/update domain is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan.exe child tree, and block the destination at egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 process spawns on the same host/timeframe, sweep synced workspace peers for the same data/storage/av JSON payload, and confirm SiYuan is upgraded to >= 3.7.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
